Ancient Indian history

Ancient Indian history: from prehistory to 1200 CE

By @archaeologywala for Talaash Heritage · Updated 15 October 2026

Ancient Indian history runs from the first stone tools, more than a million years ago, through the Indus Valley Civilization (about 2600 to 1900 BCE), the Vedic age, the Mahajanapadas, the Mauryan and Gupta empires and the regional kingdoms of the early medieval period, up to about 1200 CE. It is reconstructed from archaeology, inscriptions, coins and texts.

We teach ancient Indian history through evidence: lectures, museum sessions, Brahmi and coin workshops, and site visits such as Rakhigarhi, arranged for your group.

What counts as ancient Indian history?

Historians of India usually divide the past into ancient, medieval and modern, a scheme inherited from 19th century writing. There is no fixed line between them, but most textbooks take ancient Indian history from prehistory up to roughly the 7th or 8th century CE, and treat about 600 to 1200 CE as the early medieval period. This guide covers the whole span up to around 1200 CE, when the Delhi Sultanate was founded.

The term 'ancient India' here means the Indian subcontinent, which includes present-day Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal and parts of Afghanistan. Many key sites, such as Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Taxila and Lumbini, now lie outside the Republic of India.

For a quick reference, our Indian history timeline sets out the whole sequence up to the present, and the major dynasties of ancient India explainer lists rulers and capitals.

Sources of ancient Indian history

Ancient Indian history is built from two kinds of evidence. Archaeological sources include excavated sites, buildings, pottery, tools, bones, seeds, sculpture, inscriptions and coins. Literary sources include the Vedas, the epics, the Puranas, Buddhist and Jain canons, Sangam poetry in Tamil, technical texts such as the Arthashastra, plays, poems and the accounts of foreign visitors such as Megasthenes, Faxian and Xuanzang.

Each type has limits. Religious texts were composed and edited over centuries, so their dates are often debated. Inscriptions are precise but usually record what kings wanted remembered. Archaeology reaches ordinary people but needs careful dating. Good history uses them together and is open about what is uncertain. Our talk on excavation headlines shows how to judge claims about new discoveries.

Prehistory: the Stone Age in India

India has one of the longest prehistoric records in the world. Hand axes from Attirampakkam near Chennai have been dated to around 1.5 million years ago. Later Stone Age sites show changes in tool making, and the arrival of anatomically modern humans in South Asia is placed by most scholars somewhere between about 70,000 and 50,000 years ago, though some argue for earlier dates.

By the Mesolithic, people made tiny stone blades called microliths and painted rock shelters such as those at Bhimbetka. Farming appears at Mehrgarh in Balochistan by about 7000 BCE, with wheat, barley, cattle, sheep and goats. In the Ganga valley, the Deccan and the south, farming communities developed along their own lines. Our explainers on the Stone Age in India and rock art in India go into detail, and the lecture From stone tools to the first villages covers this span for students.

The Indus Valley Civilization

The Indus Valley Civilization, also called the Harappan Civilisation, was the largest of the Bronze Age urban cultures. At its peak, around 2600 to 1900 BCE, it covered much of present-day Pakistan and north-western India. Its cities, including Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi, Kalibangan and Lothal, had planned streets, covered drains, standardised bricks and weights, and seals carrying a script that has not been deciphered.

The cities declined after about 1900 BCE, probably because of a mix of shifting rivers, a weaker monsoon and the breakdown of long-distance trade, rather than a single invasion. Village life continued in many regions. Ancient DNA studies of a Rakhigarhi burial and other remains have added new evidence about population history, and the interpretation of that evidence is still debated. Our session on ancient DNA and the Harappan debate sets out the positions, and a visit to Rakhigarhi shows one of the largest Harappan sites in India.

The Vedic period

The Vedic period takes its name from the Vedas, the oldest texts in an Indo-European language from South Asia. The Rigveda is usually dated to around 1500 to 1200 BCE on linguistic grounds, and the later Vedic texts to about 1000 to 500 BCE. The early texts reflect a pastoral society in the north-west; the later ones show settled agriculture in the Ganga plains, the growth of kingship and the ritual and social order that would shape later Indian society.

How Indo-European languages reached South Asia is one of the most contested questions in Indian history. Linguistic evidence and recent ancient DNA studies are read by most scholars as pointing to the arrival of people with steppe ancestry in the second millennium BCE, mixing with existing populations. Others argue for an earlier or indigenous origin. A fair account presents the evidence and lets readers weigh it.

Mahajanapadas, the Buddha and the rise of Magadha

By the 6th century BCE, Buddhist and Jain texts list sixteen great states, the Mahajanapadas, stretching from Gandhara to Anga. This was the age of the second urbanisation, with fortified towns, punch-marked coins and a new class of merchants. It was also an age of new religious and philosophical movements, including those of the Buddha and Mahavira, which challenged Vedic ritual.

Magadha, in present-day Bihar, emerged as the strongest of these states under the Haryanka, Shishunaga and Nanda dynasties. Its rich farmland, iron ore and river routes gave it an edge, and its capital at Pataliputra (modern Patna) became the centre of the first empire.

The Mauryan Empire and Ashoka

The Mauryan Empire was founded by Chandragupta Maurya around 321 BCE and reached its greatest extent under his grandson Ashoka (Aśoka), who ruled from about 268 to 232 BCE. It covered almost the whole subcontinent except the far south.

Ashoka is known mainly from his own words. After the war in Kalinga he issued edicts on rocks and pillars, in Prakrit written in the Brahmi script in most of India and in Kharosthi, Greek and Aramaic in the north-west, promoting what he called dhamma. These are the earliest deciphered written records from India. James Prinsep's decipherment of Brahmi in 1837 opened them to modern readers, and our Brahmi workshop lets students read and write the script themselves.

After the Mauryas: Satavahanas, Kushanas and the Sangam age

After the Mauryas, northern and central India split among the Shungas, Indo-Greeks, Shakas and Kushanas, while the Satavahanas ruled the Deccan. This was a period of busy trade with the Roman world and Central Asia, of Buddhist stupas at Sanchi, Bharhut and Amaravati, of rock-cut monasteries in the Western Ghats, and of the Gandhara and Mathura schools of sculpture, where the Buddha first appears in human form.

In the far south, the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas are known from Sangam poetry in Tamil and from Ashoka's edicts. Excavations at Arikamedu near Puducherry, Keeladi near Madurai and Pattanam in Kerala have shown urban settlements, trade and literacy in Tamil Brahmi in the centuries around the turn of the era.

The Gupta age

The Gupta Empire, founded around 320 CE, ruled much of northern India until the mid 6th century. Older writing called it a 'golden age'; modern historians are more cautious, but the period did produce classical Sanskrit literature, including the works of Kalidasa, advances in mathematics and astronomy associated with Aryabhata, fine gold coins and some of the earliest surviving structural temples, at Sanchi, Deogarh and Bhitargaon. The Udayagiri caves near Vidisha carry Gupta inscriptions and a celebrated Varaha panel.

The Ajanta caves in Maharashtra, with their paintings, belong mostly to the late 5th century under the Vakatakas, allies of the Guptas. A visit to the Udayagiri caves is one of the best ways to see Gupta-period art in its setting.

Early medieval India: regional kingdoms and temples

From about 600 CE, power shifted to regional kingdoms: the Chalukyas of Badami, the Pallavas of Kanchipuram, the Rashtrakutas, the Pratiharas, the Palas of Bengal and Bihar, and later the Chola dynasty, which at its height in the 11th century sent naval expeditions to Southeast Asia. Land grants to Brahmins and temples, recorded on copper plates, spread agriculture and new social arrangements into forested regions.

This was the great age of temple building, from Ellora and Pattadakal to Khajuraho, Bhubaneswar and Thanjavur. Buddhist learning flourished at Nalanda and Vikramashila under Pala patronage. Arab merchants settled on the western coast, and the Ghaznavid raids of the early 11th century were followed by Ghurid campaigns in the late 12th century that led to the founding of the Delhi Sultanate, where this guide ends.

How to study ancient Indian history

Start with one good textbook, such as the NCERT books or Upinder Singh's A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India, and keep a timeline beside you. Then go to the evidence: visit a museum gallery, look at an inscription, hold a replica coin. Students preparing for civil services exams can follow our guide on how to study ancient Indian history for UPSC.

Talaash Heritage runs a lecture series that follows this sequence, from the first cities to scripts, coins and temples, with a museum gallery study to see the objects up close.

Questions people ask

What are the main periods of ancient Indian history?

The usual sequence is prehistory (Palaeolithic, Mesolithic, Neolithic and Chalcolithic), the Harappan or Indus Civilisation, the Vedic period, the age of the Mahajanapadas, the Mauryan Empire, the post-Mauryan kingdoms, the Gupta period and the early medieval regional kingdoms, ending around 1200 CE.

What are the sources of ancient Indian history?

Archaeological sources include excavated sites, monuments, pottery, tools, sculpture, inscriptions and coins. Literary sources include the Vedas, epics, Puranas, Buddhist and Jain texts, Sangam poetry, the Arthashastra, plays and the accounts of travellers such as Megasthenes, Faxian and Xuanzang.

When did ancient Indian history start?

It starts with the earliest human presence in the subcontinent. Stone tools from Attirampakkam in Tamil Nadu are dated to around 1.5 million years ago. Written history begins much later, with Ashoka's inscriptions in the 3rd century BCE, since the Harappan script is still undeciphered.

Who was the greatest ruler of ancient India?

Historians avoid ranking rulers, but Chandragupta Maurya, Ashoka, Samudragupta, Harsha and Rajaraja Chola are often discussed. Ashoka is the best documented because of his own inscriptions, which describe his policies in his own voice.

Why was the Gupta period called a golden age?

Older historians used the phrase because of the period's Sanskrit literature, mathematics, astronomy, sculpture and gold coinage. Modern historians use it less, pointing out that achievements were spread across several centuries and regions and that the term overlooks social inequality.

What caused the decline of the Indus Valley Civilization?

No single cause is accepted. Most scholars point to a combination of factors after about 1900 BCE: changes in river courses, a weaker monsoon, the drying of the Ghaggar-Hakra system and the collapse of long-distance trade. The older theory of an Aryan invasion destroying the cities is no longer supported by evidence.

Is ancient Indian history important for UPSC?

Yes. Ancient history and art and culture appear in both the Prelims and Mains papers. Questions often draw on sources, inscriptions, Buddhist and Jain history, temple architecture and the Mauryan and Gupta periods.
